translation: Aristotle, and likewise Theophrastus too, have stated precisely what one must look to in supposing a nature to be either well-tempered or ill-tempered; but these men do not even know this, and when they hear them saying that the animal is moist and hot, or that the mixture of the child is moist and hot, they neither understand how these things are said, and they recklessly transfer the account to the seasons, as though it were the same thing, and not widely different, whether one's own mixture is moist and hot or that of the air surrounding us; for it is not the same thing, nor is the mixture of an animal said to be moist and hot in the same way as the air is said to be so by a moist and hot mixture. What the cause of all these errors was I shall now relate, and I shall show clearly to those willing to apply their minds how small slips among the

the same thing, either to evacuate some moisture scattered in certain regions or to render the proper mixture drier; for an uneven dyscrasia arises in the inflamed parts, the homoeomerous bodies not yet having departed from their proper nature but still being changed and altered, while all the intervening spaces have been filled with the flux. All things, then, that are hot and moist in their mixture, when applied to parts so disposed, evacuate that superfluity which has occupied the intervening spaces of the homoeomerous bodies, but are so far from drying the bodies themselves that they even add moisture to them. The truth, then, stands thus; but what has been said requires a demonstration, which, deeming it both longer than to be appended in the present discourse and moreover requiring a hearer who understands the power of drugs, I defer for the

indeed, also with rose cerate it helps greatly; against which indeed, and against such conditions, many other drugs too will be described in the discourse that follows, some having a power similar to the date plaster, some even more active. But against rheumatic conditions this is the best drug of all, and it has often accomplished something beyond hope. Once, then, when a thigh had suppurated near the groin, the inflammation over the whole of it being unconcocted, the leg was positioned by us so that the ichors would flow out toward the groin and through the ulcer that had formed; and this having come about over a longer time, the flux that had descended into the thigh was indeed evacuated, but a fistulous condition arose beneath the skin along the whole thigh, so that one wished to divide it near the patella, in order that there should be an outflow for the ichors on either side

concerning nourishment, that the bad and the not-bad are spoken of as in relation to something, and evidently the harmful and the beneficial likewise. For in another sense you might say that the Attalic plaster is better than this plaster, because that one is more widely useful. Indeed Asclepiades himself, writing next after this one now described that very plaster made with white pepper, does not call it Attalic but Pamphilian, being ignorant, as I think, of the man who first discovered it, and having added instead the name of the man who used it and gave it to him. At any rate he wrote its promise word for word thus: 'Another, called Pamphilian, a successful drug. It works against old and hard-to-heal ulcers, carbuncles, epinyctides, achores, scabby conditions; it glues together sinuses; it works against abscesses and condylomata; and the drug is nearly more widely useful.' He says it is composed of ceruse

let each of these be done exactly, for the sake of contributing something to the whiteness of the drug. And concerning the ceruse it has been said before, and concerning the oil and the manner of boiling and the surrounding air and the fire, how each of them may contribute something to the whiteness. And just as in the case of the others, so also in the case of these, one must, knowing the powers of water and of vinegar and of sea-water and of the whitest wine, mix into the composition what is most useful for the condition being treated. For in the case of ulcers with raised banks, which have lips that are thick and hard and in need of much thinning, the ingredients levigated with vinegar and sea-water are more useful than those with water; but in those where the moisture carried in the ulcers is acrid and biting, they must rather be levigated in water

each of the metallic substances, just as again rather in wine in those cases where the moisture flowing onto the ulcers appears abundant. Each of these, then, that I have mentioned, having been levigated in each of the said liquids for several days, I threw in on each occasion into the drugs made of ceruse and litharge, and I found by trial that all of them cicatrize most excellently; and I also gave certain recipes to friends who asked for such drugs, by whom too, when they were brought to the test, they were shown to preserve their promise. So when the litharge has been boiled beforehand, as has been said, with the ceruse, and the drug has come near to a non-staining consistency, one must add the larch resin or the terebinth resin together with the white wax, and when these have been well united, throw in on top the metallic substances, keeping the following proportion: of litharge and ceruse, according to the usual practice, a pound of each with two pounds of oil; let it be boiled repeatedly

but if something scirrhous of its inflammation should remain, to apply some of the things that dry sufficiently. Since, then, something appeared to be left over, I used first the drug made with the root of dracontium, which has the other ingredients the same as the Egyptian drug called Isis, but has taken in addition the root of dracontium; and next after this, having used the one called Athena, from that I went on thereafter to the cicatrizing agents. In another case, anointing the denuded parts of the wound with the troche dissolved in boiled-down must, I applied on the outside the euphorbium, having mixed it with wax and resin in such a quantity that it should at once become plaster-like and preserve the power of the euphorbium. How one, looking to these aims, should compound the drug I shall say next; for indeed I also made another drug with vinegar

just as to the resin and the pitch; for this reason I mix with the cerate resin or pitch or a part of each. It is quite clear, then, that when these are mixed in, the oil is no longer to be put in equal to them; for wax needs much of the fat to attain moistness, whereas among the resins the dry ones need altogether little, and the moist ones even want to take on some dry substance in order to reach a plaster-like consistency. Now among the waxes the difference in respect of moistness and dryness is not great; but with the resins, on the contrary, just as with pitch, the difference between the dry and the moist is very great. The driest of the resins, then, is the one which some call fried, others colophony; second is the one from the potteries, unpurified and unfried; but if one purifies it

you have seen me doing throughout, not in the case of this alone but also of the ammoniac incense. The drug written after this one by the Tarentine is also of the same promise, according to the following proportion: of chalcitis 25 drachms, of cadmia 12 drachms; having levigated them separately and mixed in unadulterated wine and brought it to the boil, pour it on so that they are kneaded in due measure; then levigate until it is dried; and having melted 50 drachms of wax, 30 drachms of terebinth resin, 8 cotylae of myrtle oil, mix with the cerate 20 drachms of the dry ingredients. And this drug has none of the emollient ingredients; however, in the mixing with the cerate, one trained rationally in the methods which I have set out would suitably work out the quantity of the mixture proper for each of the ulcers. And rightly too he specifies the unadulterated wine, that is, wine with which sea-water has not been mixed

the meltable ingredients, having let them cool somewhat, sprinkle the dry ingredients over these, stirring carefully. One must have ready, ground with vinegar, myrrh, frankincense, bdellium, opopanax; and into these are thrown the contents of the pan, and it is ground so that no wax-lumps form; and when it is in good condition, take it up into a wooden box previously smeared inside with iris oil. On the third kind of ulcers hard to treat, about which Asclepiades wrote word for word as follows: 'In the case of ulcers that do not close at all, or that close but break down again, either with the flesh being corrupted or even with the underlying bones having been destroyed, one must use the preparations set out below. Against chironian and hard-to-heal ulcers, a successful drug: of scale of copper, of scraped verdigris, one ounce each; of wax, half a pound; of larch resin, one and a half ounces; pour the meltable ingredients over the dry, and having taken it up, use it, kneading carefully and applying a small flat piece over

the metallic substances with vinegar, and after these adding the dry ingredients and levigating again; then, when these have a mud-like consistency, mixing in the meltable ingredients as has been said before. Another: of asphalt and of terebinth resin and of Bruttian pitch, one pound each; of oil, 24 drachms; of litharge and ceruse and manna and verdigris and scale and opopanax, of each an amount equal to the twenty-four drachms of the oil; of ladanum two ounces, which is 16 drachms; and two cotylae of vinegar. This drug too is prepared in the same way as the two before it. Another: of chrysocolla and scale and steel, 4 drachms each; of verdigris and of chalcanthum, half of each, that is 2 drachms each; of wax, 25 drachms, that is 3 ounces and one drachm; of terebinth resin, 2 ounces, that is 16 drachms. Melt the wax with the terebinth

Of verdigris of copper and of Indian aloe, of burnt copper and of good diphryges, sixteen and a half from each ingredient; twenty drachms of galbanum and four; of manna of frankincense the same, twice 12; of ammoniac twice 5 and twice 20; sixteen drachms of Attic propolis; of long aristolochia twice 10 drachms; twice 6 drachms of scale of Cyprian copper; and of the driest gentian root an equal amount. To all these add in addition of dry dittany herb, having its flower, 20 holkai, finely ground. of wax, having neither of these, but the ammoniac incense alone, when put in, will make the drug parched. But for plaster-making, for it is no worse to name it thus, both the wax and the resin are useful; for the softening and the dispersing belong to the drug through the ammoniac alone, which holds first place among the emollients and is a rival also to the discutients. And having recalled what was said in the fifth book of The Powers of Simple Drugs, as to what sort of mixture such drugs must have, you will no longer need any further teaching. For the primary powers active in drugs lie in heat and cold and moisture and dryness; the secondary are the emollient and discutient and repellent and attractive and concoctive and detergent and septic, just as also

of all the ingredients carefully; again let a little drip off; if you see it well-coloured and well-blended, take the pot at once from the fire and add galbanum, previously softened. But if the drug is by far too hard, add oil to it to a good blend. Having thus strained it, then into another vessel, cold, knead it with the hands and so store it away. I shall write below another, of the same kind as the one before it. It works against the affections I mentioned before; this one cicatrizes better than all drugs ulcers hard to heal, callous and chronic; the eruptions arising on the face this one cures without any harmful biting; and the fissures and hardnesses that the seat has, the condyloid ones, and calluses it casts off. Prepare it thus: a mina of good litharge, and a mina is a pound and a third part of a pound; of good Pontic wax half a mina; of good scraped verdigris a quarter part of a mina

scrofulous swellings, repressing every oedema, and healing the watery conditions of the liver and of the spleen, drawing copious excretions of urine; it also dissolves sciatic affections that have become chronic. Using this, Ulpianus, a well-endowed young man, benefited very many. It contains one pound of Pontic wax, one of fried resin and one of pine resin, one ounce of fresh quicklime, one ounce of fissile alum, and of Pontic arsenic an amount equal to one of these. Having poured over these a little fragrant vinegar, levigate for a sufficient time in a larger mortar; then, having added a little oil to the wax and resin and melted them over the fierce flame of a fire, and mixing all carefully, and making malagmata of non-staining thickness, keep it stored away, using it where needed as a fresh compress. And the most excellent man, the father of the drug, used to say that also for deliverance from long diseases

which also heal small inflammations. Of the compound emollients, some are, as one might say, weaker, in the first rank; some not much stronger than these, in the second; and certain others in the third; and besides these, others in the fourth. And one ought to use them, as has been said before, against slight hardnesses and soft bodies those of the first rank, and against bodies and affections stronger than these those of the second, just as also those of the third and the fourth proportionately. They also set out separately those under each of them.
